title: THE FAMILY SECRETS, FORBIDDEN DESIRES, AND SEXUAL SCANDALS GOD REFUSED TO ERASE FROM THE BIBLE
paragraphs: THE FAMILY SECRETS, FORBIDDEN DESIRES, AND SEXUAL SCANDALS GOD REFUSED TO ERASE FROM THE BIBLE

From incest and prostitution to royal concubines, dangerous seduction, and passionate marriage poetry—why would a holy God preserve such uncomfortable stories in His Word? The answer may change how you see your own past, your deepest struggles, and the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
There are things families refuse to talk about.
Things buried beneath respectable last names. Things whispered behind closed doors. Things that happened years ago but somehow still haunt the people who never even witnessed them.
A pregnancy nobody wants explained.
A betrayal everyone pretends never happened.
A marriage that looks beautiful in photographs but is collapsing behind the walls.
A child carrying shame that never belonged to them.
A secret desire. A forbidden relationship. A moment of weakness that became a lifetime of consequences.
And sometimes, the people carrying these stories are sitting in church every Sunday.
Smiling.
Singing.
Lifting their hands in worship.
While silently wondering whether God could ever look at the whole truth about their lives and still love them.
But here is something that might surprise you.
God already knows the worst chapters of human history. And He deliberately allowed some of them to be recorded in the Bible.
Not because He celebrates wickedness.
Not because He excuses exploitation.
Not because every relationship described in Scripture receives His approval.
But because the God who saves sinners has never needed a sanitized version of humanity to reveal the glory of His grace.
Open your Bible.
You will find incestuous family histories, prostitution, adultery, sexual violence, royal concubines, seduction, polygamy, and marriages devastated by betrayal.
You will also find breathtaking poetry celebrating the beauty of marital love.

And standing above all these complicated human stories is a holy God who refuses to confuse love with lust, desire with entitlement, forgiveness with permission, or grace with the absence of consequences.
The Bible is not embarrassed by the truth.
Perhaps the more uncomfortable question is why we are so determined to hide ours.
Consider Lot.

He had survived the destruction of Sodom. He had witnessed judgment upon a city infamous for its wickedness. He had escaped with his daughters, yet his family was already carrying the devastation of everything they had lost.
Then Genesis 19 records one of the most disturbing family episodes in Scripture.
Lot's daughters made their father drunk and had sexual relations with him while he was unaware of what was happening.
The account connects those pregnancies with the origins of Moab and Ammon.
Read it carefully.
There is no command from God approving what happened. No divine celebration of incest. No suggestion that desperation turns wrongdoing into righteousness.
And the intoxicated father is not presented as knowingly consenting to those encounters.
Scripture records the event without requiring us to defend it.
This distinction matters enormously.
The Bible describing an action is not the same as God endorsing that action.
There are people today who have suffered violations within their own families, sometimes at the hands of people who were supposed to protect them.
If that is part of your history, hear this clearly.
What someone did to you does not make you spiritually contaminated.
Their wrongdoing is not your guilt.
Your worth was never surrendered to the person who violated your trust.
And the God who sees what happened does not demand that you pretend it was harmless.
Healing may require safety, truthful disclosure, wise pastoral care, professional support, and accountability for those responsible.
Forgiveness must never be twisted into permission for abuse to continue.
God's grace does not require victims to deny the truth.
But the story does not end in that cave.
Centuries later, a woman named Ruth appears.
She is a Moabite.
And suddenly, one of the peoples connected to that painful Genesis history becomes part of a much larger redemptive story.
Ruth follows Naomi into Bethlehem. She chooses loyalty over abandonment. She trusts the God of Israel.
And eventually, Ruth marries Boaz.
Their son is Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And Matthew's Gospel places Ruth within the ancestry leading to Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A woman from Moab becomes an honored figure in the family history of Israel's greatest king and, ultimately, in the earthly genealogy of the Messiah.
This does not mean God approved the wrongdoing recorded in Genesis 19.
It means that a people's painful origin does not place every future generation beyond the reach of His mercy.
Your family history may explain where you came from. It does not have the authority to decide what God's grace can make of your life.
And if that already challenges the way you see your past, wait until you meet Tamar.
Genesis 38 introduces a woman whose story is filled with bereavement, injustice, withheld responsibility, deception, and a sexual encounter that exposes a powerful man's hypocrisy.
Tamar had been married into Judah's family.
Her first husband died.
Her second husband also died after acting wickedly.
Judah then withheld the remaining son he had promised would eventually become her husband, leaving Tamar in a vulnerable position within the social and family structures of that time.
Eventually, Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute and Judah had relations with her without recognizing her.
When her pregnancy became known, Judah initially demanded punishment.
Then the evidence revealed that he himself was the father.
And Judah said something extraordinary.
In the Hebrew text of Genesis 38:26, he acknowledges:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tsadeqah mimmenni.
A close translation is, "She is more righteous than I."
Not because every part of Tamar's strategy should be copied.
Not because sexual deception becomes a universal model of righteousness.
But because Judah recognized his own failure and the injustice he had committed against her.
The man who was ready to condemn a woman had to confront the wrongdoing he had been hiding.
Does that sound familiar?
How quickly people can demand judgment for the sins they can see while protecting the sins they have learned to conceal.
How easily religious language can become a shield for personal hypocrisy.
And yet Tamar's story does not disappear from the biblical record.
Matthew 1:3 explicitly names her in the genealogy of Jesus.
Perez, one of the sons born from that encounter, becomes an ancestor in the line leading to David and ultimately to Christ.
God did not need to rewrite the historical record to make the Messiah's ancestry look more respectable.
He preserved the truth.
Not to glorify the scandal.
But to show that human failure could not overthrow His redemptive purpose.
And then there is Rahab.
A woman introduced in Joshua 2 as a prostitute living in Jericho.
In Hebrew, the word used to describe her is:
זוֹנָה
Zonah.
The word ordinarily means a prostitute.
Scripture does not need to pretend she had a different occupation to make her story acceptable.
Rahab lived in a city facing judgment, yet she recognized that the God of Israel was truly God.
She protected the Israelite spies and asked that her family be spared.
Her confession in Joshua 2:11 is remarkable.
She acknowledges the LORD as God in heaven above and on earth beneath.
Her past is part of her story.
But it is not the final word about her faith.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers Rahab among those who acted by faith.
James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of living faith.
And Matthew 1:5 names Rahab in the genealogy of Jesus.
Imagine that.
A woman once identified by prostitution is remembered in the New Testament for faith.
Not because prostitution itself was celebrated.
Not because God reclassified every past action as righteous.
But because faith in the living God mattered more than the identity by which society had known her.
Some people spend their entire lives terrified that their worst chapter will become their permanent name.
The adulterer.
The addict.
The abandoned woman.
The person with the ruined marriage.
The one whose past everyone knows.
But Rahab's story asks a question that reaches beyond Jericho.
What happens when God begins writing a future that your old reputation never could have predicted?
Then Scripture takes us into the royal courts of Israel.
And the stories become even more uncomfortable.
Kings had wives.
Kings had concubines.
Kings formed households that reflected the power arrangements of their world.
The Hebrew word often translated "concubine" is פִּילֶגֶשׁ, pilegesh.
It refers to a woman in a recognized but generally secondary marital or household relationship, whose social position and protections could differ from those of a principal wife.
These relationships existed in the ancient world.
But their presence in biblical narratives does not make them God's ideal for marriage.
Genesis 2:24 presents the foundational pattern of a man and his wife becoming one flesh.
Jesus returns to that creation account in Matthew 19:4–6 when teaching about marriage.
The fact that powerful men accumulated women does not mean the Creator commanded them to do so.
In fact, Deuteronomy 17:17 warns Israel's king against multiplying wives for himself.
And when you read the stories of the royal households, you begin to understand why.
David's family became fractured by sexual wrongdoing, violence, rivalry, and devastating grief.
In 2 Samuel 13, Amnon violated his half-sister Tamar despite her resistance.
The account portrays an act of sexual violence, not a romantic encounter.
Tamar's protest and suffering matter.
Her story should never be softened into a tale of forbidden passion.
There is a profound difference between love and possession.
Between affection and coercion.
Between desire and the decision to disregard another person's dignity.
A desire that refuses to respect another person's humanity is not made holy simply because it feels powerful.
Later, Absalom publicly took his father's concubines as part of his rebellion, fulfilling a devastating prophetic judgment recorded in 2 Samuel 12:11–12 and narrated in 2 Samuel 16:21–22.
These women were caught in a struggle for royal power.
Their vulnerability should not be overlooked.
The narrative is not an invitation to admire the spectacle.
It reveals how ambition, humiliation, and the abuse of power can turn human beings into instruments of revenge.
And Solomon?
The king associated with extraordinary wisdom accumulated seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, according to 1 Kings 11:3.
Yet Scripture explicitly says his wives turned his heart away.
What the world might have interpreted as status and abundance became part of his spiritual downfall.
One thousand women did not produce one thousand measures of faithfulness.
Royal privilege could not protect a divided heart.
And there is a lesson here that reaches directly into modern life.
You can have access to more people, more attention, more opportunities, and more pleasure than previous generations ever imagined.
You can carry an entire world of temptation inside a phone.
You can be admired publicly and spiritually empty privately.
You can be surrounded by people and still be profoundly lonely.
The human heart cannot be healed merely by giving it more of everything it desires.
David himself knew the devastation of desire left unchecked.
He saw Bathsheba bathing.
He sent for her.
He slept with her.
And when she became pregnant, he attempted to conceal what had happened.
Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah, one of David's soldiers.
David was the king.
That imbalance of power must not be ignored.
The text does not give us grounds to treat Bathsheba as the architect of David's wrongdoing.
Scripture places grave responsibility upon David, who used his position, arranged Uriah's death, and took Bathsheba as his wife.
Second Samuel 11:27 declares that what David had done displeased the LORD.
The prophet Nathan confronted him.
David confessed.
And although God showed mercy, the consequences were devastating.
The child born from that pregnancy died.
David's household continued to experience terrible suffering.
Repentance was real.
Forgiveness was real.
But forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
That is a truth many people would rather avoid.
We sometimes want grace to mean that nothing painful follows our choices.
We want repentance without confession.
Restoration without accountability.
Mercy without truth.
But biblical grace is not the art of pretending sin was harmless.
It is the mercy of God meeting sinners in the truth.
Psalm 51 gives voice to David's repentance.
In Psalm 51:10, the Hebrew reads:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God."
Notice what David asks for.
Not merely a repaired reputation.
Not a more convincing explanation.
Not a way to silence Nathan.
A clean heart.
He knows the problem runs deeper than public exposure.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are not afraid of being guilty.
We are afraid of being discovered.
We know how to look faithful.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know how to speak about holiness.
But when nobody is watching, we return to the same habits, the same conversations, the same secret compromises.
And then we wonder why our souls feel exhausted.
The Gospel does not invite us to become better actors.
It invites us to come into the light.
But here is where the Bible surprises us again.
After all these painful accounts of distorted desire, Scripture gives us a book filled with passionate love poetry.
The Song of Songs.
In Hebrew, its title begins:
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים
Shir haShirim.
Literally, "Song of Songs"—a Hebrew expression conveying the excellence of the song.
And its language is tender, poetic, intimate, and at times strikingly sensual.
The lovers express longing.
They admire one another.
They delight in physical beauty.
They anticipate closeness.
They speak in images drawn from gardens, vineyards, spices, flowers, and the natural world.
Song of Songs 8:7 declares, in a close translation of the Hebrew:
"Many waters cannot extinguish love, and rivers cannot sweep it away."
Think about what this means.
The same Bible that exposes adultery and condemns sexual exploitation also preserves poetry celebrating romantic desire.
Why?
Because human desire itself is not automatically evil.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
Marriage is not presented in Scripture merely as a legal arrangement without affection.
The biblical vision includes covenant, faithfulness, mutual belonging, and delight.
Desire becomes destructive when it is detached from truth, faithfulness, and love of neighbor.
It becomes dangerous when another person is reduced to an object.
When pleasure becomes more important than integrity.
When secrecy replaces honesty.
When the pursuit of satisfaction tramples the dignity of another human being.
But desire expressed faithfully within God's design for marriage is not something believers need to regard as inherently shameful.
The Song of Songs has also been read by Jewish and Christian interpreters as expressing deeper truths about divine love.
Yet its poetic celebration of human love should not be erased in the process.
God does not need to deny the goodness of creation in order to teach us holiness.
Holiness is not the destruction of everything human. It is the surrender of our humanity to the One who created it.
And now we come to the most astonishing part of all.
Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy.
For many readers, genealogies are the pages they hurry past.
Names.
Generations.
Fathers.
Sons.
History.
But hidden in that list are reminders of some of the stories we have just encountered.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
And the wife of Uriah.
Matthew does not even name Bathsheba in that particular reference.
He calls attention to her connection with Uriah, preserving the memory of the marriage David violated.
It is as though the genealogy refuses to let royal history become a polished public-relations campaign.
There are stories here that no human family would choose for its official portrait.
And yet the genealogy moves steadily toward Jesus.
The Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The One whose coming was not prevented by the failures of those who came before Him.
But do not misunderstand this.
Jesus did not come because sin was beautiful.
He came because sinners needed a Savior.
He did not come to baptize human rebellion with religious language.
He came to redeem.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to do what no human being could accomplish through self-improvement alone.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than a motivational message about overcoming your past.
Jesus Christ is not merely offering you a better self-image.
He is offering reconciliation with God through His death and resurrection.
The Son of God entered our broken world without participating in its sin.
He was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, according to 1 Peter 2:24.
And He rose again.
Not simply to make people feel forgiven.
But to accomplish the salvation that human beings could never earn.
When Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 about patterns of unrighteousness, he does not pretend sin is unimportant.
He names serious sins and warns against continuing in unrighteousness.
Then he writes something extraordinary:
And he goes on to speak of believers being washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:11 includes:
ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε
Alla apelousasthe.
"But you were washed."
The verb communicates cleansing, and in this passage it belongs to Paul's description of the decisive change associated with belonging to Christ.
He is not saying that every struggle instantly disappeared.
He is not saying that believers never need repentance again.
He is saying that their former sinful identities no longer have the final authority over who they are in Christ.
That is the difference between religious performance and redemption.
Religion without the Gospel can teach you how to conceal the stain.
Christ offers cleansing.
Religion without grace can make you terrified of exposure.
Christ calls you into truthful repentance and forgiveness.
Religion without transformation can leave you outwardly respectable and inwardly enslaved.
Christ gives His people the Holy Spirit and calls them to walk in newness of life.
And maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret nobody knows.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by betrayal.
Maybe pornography has become a habit you keep promising to abandon.
Maybe you are wrestling with desires you do not know how to surrender.
Maybe someone exploited you, and you have spent years blaming yourself.
Maybe your family history is filled with abandonment, violence, infidelity, or shame.
Or maybe your greatest struggle is not something the world would call scandalous.
Maybe it is pride.
Self-righteousness.
A judgmental heart.
The quiet pleasure of seeing another person's sin exposed while your own remains hidden.
Whatever brought you here, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work of conviction calls us toward truth and Christ.
It is not an invitation to despair.
There is a difference between saying, "I have sinned," and believing, "I am beyond the reach of God's mercy."
The first can become the beginning of repentance.
The second denies the sufficiency of the Savior.
And for those who have been sinned against, the call is not to confess responsibility for another person's evil.
It is to know that Christ sees your suffering, values your dignity, and offers hope without requiring you to excuse injustice.
The cross speaks both of the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable mercy of God.
At Calvary, grace was not cheap.
Our redemption was purchased at the cost of Christ's own life.
And the empty tomb declares that death did not have the final word.
So why do we keep behaving as though our past is more powerful than the risen Jesus?
Why do we keep hiding from the One who already knows us?
Why do we keep returning to the very things that are destroying our peace?
Why do we sometimes prefer the appearance of holiness to the difficult beauty of actual repentance?
There is a moment in John 8 when a woman accused of adultery stands before Jesus, surrounded by men eager to condemn her.

The passage of John 7:53–8:11 has a well-known textual-history question: it is absent from many of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. It has nevertheless been received in many Christian traditions as a treasured account, and its themes accord with Jesus' clearly attested mercy toward sinners and His call to repentance.
In the familiar account, Jesus says:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
Notice both parts.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Jesus does not treat the woman as disposable.
Neither does He describe adultery as harmless.
He refuses to make condemnation the end of her story.
And He calls her toward a different life.
This is the Christ-centered balance we desperately need.
Truth without cruelty.
Grace without compromise.
Repentance without despair.
Forgiveness without pretending consequences do not exist.
Love without exploitation.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
And hope grounded not in human perfection, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
If this article has touched a place you normally keep hidden, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than another quick reaction on social media.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to disclose private trauma or personal sins publicly to prove your sincerity. But if you want someone to pray with you, you can comment, "Christ is still healing me."
And if your testimony is that Jesus has brought you out of a painful past, consider sharing a few words about His faithfulness. Someone reading the comments may need to know that change is possible.
There may be a person in your family who believes they have already ruined their life.
A friend who has quietly abandoned church because of shame.
A husband or wife struggling to rebuild trust.
A young believer who has never understood the difference between biblical desire and sinful lust.
A survivor who needs to hear that the wrong committed against them does not define their worth.
But I also want to speak to those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.
Every article requires time, research, writing, biblical care, and the ongoing work of placing these messages before readers who may never walk into a church building.
Every testimony shared, every biblical truth explained, and every struggling soul encouraged represents an opportunity to serve Christ by serving people.
It is a practical way of helping sustain and expand this work so that more people can encounter biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and resources for spiritual growth.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing, not coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says that each person should give as they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It does not replace repentance, worship, fellowship, or obedience.
And you do not have to pay to glorify God.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
It is spiritual nourishment.
It is helping make room for more biblical teaching, more encouragement, and more opportunities to point people toward Jesus.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and spiritual learning more accessible.
Because the purpose of this ministry is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to keep pointing people toward the One who died for sinners and rose again.
Why would God preserve so many uncomfortable human stories in His holy Word?
Why leave the record of Lot's family?
Why tell us about Tamar and Judah?
Why identify Rahab as a prostitute?
Why expose David's adultery and abuse of power?
Why show the ruin that followed Solomon's multiplied marriages?
Why preserve both the darkness of sexual wrongdoing and the beauty of faithful marital love?
Because Scripture tells the truth about the human condition.
Because sin is real.
Because desire matters.
Because the vulnerable matter.
Because holiness matters.
Because our choices have consequences.
And because God's redemptive purpose is greater than the human failures that appear throughout the biblical story.
But above all, because these accounts prepare us to recognize how desperately we need Jesus Christ.
The Bible is not a gallery of flawless heroes.
It is the unfolding revelation of a holy God who acts in history to redeem a people for Himself.
Its central hope is not that human beings eventually learn to hide their failures more successfully.
Its central hope is that Jesus Christ has come to save sinners.
And that means the final question is not simply whether your past is scandalous.
It is whether you will bring your life into the light of His truth.
Will you repent where repentance is needed?
Will you seek help where healing is needed?
Will you stop defending what God calls sin?
Will you stop carrying guilt for what someone else did to you?
Will you trust that the blood of Christ is sufficient to cleanse the sinner who comes to Him in faith?
Will you follow Jesus, not merely admire the idea of being forgiven?
The past cannot be undone.
Some consequences must still be faced.
Some relationships may never return to what they once were.
Some wounds require long seasons of care and healing.
But the Gospel declares that no repentant sinner needs to remain separated from God when they come to Christ in faith.
And no survivor of another person's wrongdoing needs to accept shame as their identity.
Jesus does not promise that every earthly story will become painless.
He promises something infinitely greater to those who belong to Him.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
The presence of His Spirit.
The hope of resurrection.
And a future in which sin, death, and sorrow will not reign forever.
So when the enemy of your soul tries to convince you that the worst chapter of your life is the only chapter that matters, remember the testimony of Scripture.
God did not erase the uncomfortable histories.
He revealed His saving purpose through the unfolding story that leads to Christ.
And when you are tempted to believe that your story is already finished, remember the empty tomb.
The scars may remain in your story, but they do not have to become the name by which you live forever.
